newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan links intravenous food supplements to deaths.
newsitem.headline: Japan links intravenous food supplements to deaths.

text.p: Intravenous food supplements given to patients in hospitals are believed to have caused 41 deaths since 1990, a spokesman for Japan's Health and Welfare Ministry said on Tuesday.
"We cannot deny that the 41 deaths were due to the use of the food supplement but we are investigating the exact cause of death in all these cases," he said.
The deaths were among 85 cases since 1990 in which high-calorie and electrolytic food supplements were thought to have had harmful side effects, the spokesman said.

The ministry on Monday ordered the eight domestic pharmaceutical firms which produce the infusions to supply safety information to doctors to prevent recurrences, repeating an October 1991 directive which went largely unheeded, he added.

Complications including unconsciousness, low blood pressure and memory failure may occur when high-calorie food supplements are given to patients whose bodies lack sufficient levels of vitamin B1, the spokesman said.
Some 40,000 to 50,000 people in Japan receive such high-calorie supplements every day, accounting for annual sales of 38 billion yen ($330 million), he said. ($1=115 yen)
